content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Peaches Stage 1 is a smooth puree made from ripe peaches, specially formulated for infants aged 6–12 months. The puree has a uniform texture, contains no added sugar, salt, or preservatives, making it a safe first fruit option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peaches belong to the Rosaceae family and are close relatives of plums, apricots, and cherries.
In Stage 1 puree only the flesh is used; the pit is completely removed to eliminate choking hazards.
Peaches are rich in vitamin C, which supports immunity and aids iron absorption.
The fiber content helps develop a healthy gut microbiome in babies.
Fruit purees are often introduced after vegetable purees to familiarize the child with a mildly sweet taste.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports the immune system and tissue development.

items.title: Contains beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, essential for vision and cell growth.

items.title: Low allergen potential
items.content: Peach puree rarely triggers allergic reactions, though any new food should be introduced gradually.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A modest amount of dietary fiber promotes soft stools and helps prevent constipation.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Peaches are about 85 % water, contributing to proper hydration for infants.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Although uncommon, some infants may be allergic to peaches. Monitor for any reaction when first introduced.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Peaches are naturally sweet; do not add extra sugar or combine with other sweet foods.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The mild acidity may cause slight stomach irritation in sensitive babies; choose fully ripe fruit.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the puree chilled or warmed to room temperature. It can be blended with other Stage 1 foods (e.g., carrot puree) for flavor variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened package refrigerated and use within 48 hours. After opening, transfer to an airtight container and consume within 24 hours. Discard if any off‑odor or discoloration appears.

content.title: About
content.content: The Bologna sandwich on white bread (1813) is a classic sandwich made of sliced cooked Bologna sausage, soft cream cheese, and fresh vegetables, placed between two slices of white roll. It is popular in cafés and cafeterias as a quick, satisfying snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recipe for a Bologna sausage sandwich appeared in the early 19th century in Italy.
White bread in the original recipe is chosen without a crust to let the delicate flavor of the sausage shine.
Traditionally the sandwich includes lettuce, a tomato slice, and a light spread of mustard.
In some regions the cream cheese is replaced with mozzarella to enhance the aroma.
The sandwich is often served with potato chips or pickled cucumbers.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Bologna sausage provides about 12 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meat products are rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The sausage contains vitamins B1, B2, B6 and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cream cheese adds calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Dietary fiber from vegetables
items.content: Lettuce and tomato provide a modest amount of fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed meats often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Both the cheese and the sausage contain saturated fats, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cream cheese can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some Bologna sausages contain nitrites and other preservatives, so moderate consumption is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the Bologna thinly, spread cream cheese on both sides of the bread, add lettuce and a tomato slice. Optionally spread mustard or mayonnaise. The sandwich is easy to eat by hand; you may cut it in half for serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in the refrigerator in an airtight container for no more than 24 hours. Keep the sausage and cheese separately at 2‑4 °C. For longer storage, keep ingredients separate and assemble the sandwich just before serving.

chicken-ns-as-to-part-fried-coated-skin-.title: Chicken, NS as part, fried, coated, skin/coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken prepared using the NS (non‑sieved) method is deep‑fried after a coating is applied. The skin and coating are not eaten and are usually removed before serving. This cooking style keeps the meat juicy while giving it a crisp outer layer.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The NS technique involves minimal pre‑cooking, preserving more of the meat’s natural flavor.
Deep‑frying at 175‑190 °C creates a golden crust and quickly seals in juices.
Coatings often consist of flour, spices and breadcrumbs, but they are discarded because they may contain non‑food additives.
Chicken is one of the world’s most widely consumed sources of protein.
Removing skin and coating reduces the amount of saturated fat in the final dish.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat (skin‑less)
items.content: After discarding the skin and coating, the dish contains significantly less saturated fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Chicken protein is quickly absorbed, making it suitable for people with increased nutritional needs.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Insufficient cooking can leave salmonella or campylobacter alive.

items.title: High sodium in coating
items.content: If the coating contains salt, intake should be limited for hypertension.

items.title: Trans fats in ready‑made coating
items.content: Some pre‑made batters may contain partially hydrogenated oils.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Before serving, remove the skin and coating, leaving only the tender meat. Pieces can be added to salads, served with vegetable sides, used in sandwiches, or sliced for appetizers. A light yogurt‑or lemon‑based sauce pairs well.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken chimichanga is a fried Mexican dish consisting of a tortilla filled with shredded chicken, cheese, beans, rice, and spices, then deep‑fried until golden and crispy. The result is a crunchy exterior with a flavorful, mildly spicy interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chimichanga originated in Texas, where Mexican cuisine merged with local traditions.
Traditionally the dish was wrapped in foil before frying to keep the filling moist.
In the United States it is often served with salsa, guacamole, and sour cream.
Vegetarian versions replace chicken with beans, vegetables, and cheese.
The name “chimichanga” is believed to come from a Spanish slang term meaning “mess” or “bad piece.”

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Chicken and beans supply iron, important for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish offers B6 and B12 vitamins that support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Beans and rice add dietary fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Turmeric, paprika, and chili contain antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Deep‑frying increases calories and saturated fat, which may be undesirable in excess.

items.title: Spicy flavor
items.content: Chili and spices can irritate the stomach of people with sensitive digestive systems.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese in the filling may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Cooking contaminants
items.content: Improper oil temperature can produce trans fats and acrylamide, potentially harmful compounds.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the chicken chimichanga hot, cut in half. It can be eaten with hands or a fork, accompanied by salsa, guacamole, sour cream, or tomato sauce. For a lighter option, bake instead of fry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked chimichanga in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. It can also be frozen for up to 2 months; reheat in the oven to restore crispness before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Clams are marine bivalve mollusks of the family Veneridae, found in coastal waters worldwide. They have a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a mildly crunchy texture. Clams are eaten raw (e.g., in sushi), boiled, steamed, baked, and used in soups, sauces, and pastas.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Clams can filter up to 50 liters of water per day, helping to clean their environment.
There are more than 2,000 species of clams, varying in size, shape, and shell color.
In ancient cultures clams were used as a form of currency and a symbol of abundance.
Clams can repair their shells by depositing new layers of calcium carbonate.
In some regions clams are considered a delicacy and featured in special festive dishes.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Clams provide about 12 g of protein per 100 g, making them an excellent source of lean protein.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many seafood items, clams contain very little fat, suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for blood formation and nervous system health; clams are a significant source.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function and metabolism.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Clams provide modest amounts of EPA and DHA, beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to clams, ranging from mild to anaphylactic.

items.title: Toxin contamination
items.content: Clams can accumulate heavy metals and biotoxins (e.g., domoic acid); purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Food poisoning
items.content: Raw or undercooked clams may harbor pathogenic bacteria such as Vibrio or Salmonella.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Brined or canned clams can be high in sodium, which may be problematic for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Clams can be steamed, boiled in broth, sautéed with garlic and butter, added to pasta, risotto, or soups. Raw clams are often used in sushi and ceviche after thorough cleaning and marinating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep live clams in the refrigerator in a tightly sealed container covered with a damp cloth, no more than 2‑3 days. Cooked clams store 1‑2 days in an airtight container in the fridge. Freezing is recommended only after pre‑cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Taquito is a popular Mexican street snack consisting of a soft corn or flour tortilla filled only with melted cheese. The cheese melts into a smooth, slightly aromatic filling when heated.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Taquito originated in Mexico in the early 20th century as a quick street food.
There are many variants – with meat, beans, or cheese – but the cheese‑only version is the classic vegetarian choice.
Traditionally the tortilla is grilled, giving it a light crisp on the outside.
The cheese used is often a blend of cheddar and Mexican queso fresco, providing a mild flavor and good meltability.
In the United States taquitos are commonly served with salsa or guacamole.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese is rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Protein in cheese helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese provides B2 and B12 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic cultures
items.content: Some processed cheeses retain live cultures that can benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: A cheese‑only taquito contains virtually no carbohydrates, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese contains lactose, so those who are intolerant should choose lactose‑free options.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein, the main milk protein.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed cheese often contains a lot of salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cheese is calorie‑dense; overconsumption can lead to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese taquitos are usually heated on a skillet, grill, or microwave until the cheese melts. Serve hot with salsa, guacamole, or sour cream. They can be topped with fresh vegetables such as tomatoes, avocado, or lettuce for added texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked taquitos in the refrigerator in an airtight container for 2‑3 days. Keep the cheese filling at 0‑4 °C. If frozen, both the tortilla and cheese can be kept up to 1 month, though texture may change after thawing.
